description: We are excited to join the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026!
summary:
ARTEMIS Astronauts Helper is an intuitive mission-planning and visualization platform designed to help astronauts, mission planners, and educators select optimal landing sites and dates on the lunar South Pole. Exploring the South Pole presents extreme lighting and communication constraints due to rugged crater topography, low solar angles, and lunar libration, while existing planning tools feature overly complex interfaces.
Our application transforms complex NASA topographical (LOLA) and ephemeris (JPL Horizons) datasets into a clear, interactive horizon visualizer. Users can compare candidate landing sites across different dates, view real-time Sun and Earth positions relative to local mountain ridges, and track exact countdowns to sunset and Earthset. By instantly assessing solar power windows, autonomous Fission Surface Power fallback needs, and direct-to-Earth communication availability, our platform streamlines critical mission decision-making for the Artemis era.
details:
What It Does & How It Works Landing on the Moon's South Pole is one of the toughest challenges in modern space exploration because of freezing permanent shadows, low-angle sunlight, and frequent communication blackouts. Existing planning tools get the job done, but their clunky, overly technical interfaces make comparing landing sites a slow process. We built ARTEMIS Astronauts Helper to solve this—acting like a smart "Google Maps for the Moon." Our app takes real NASA terrain data (LOLA) and tracking calculations (JPL Horizons) and turns them into a live, interactive horizon view. Users can pick any candidate landing site and date to immediately see where the Sun and Earth sit relative to local crater rims and mountains, complete with live countdowns to sunset and Earthset.

Factors Our Team Considered To make sure our planner reflects real-world Artemis mission challenges, we factored in several critical lunar constraints:

  • Power & Thermal Survival: We tracked continuous sunlight windows on Peaks of Eternal Light (PELs) versus shadow zones, building in an automatic backup simulation for Fission Surface Power (FSP) nuclear reactors whenever the Sun dips behind a mountain ridge.
  • Communication Blackouts: Because Earth wobbles in the lunar sky (lunar libration) and disappears behind terrain, we calculated direct-to-Earth signal windows and modeled LunaNet orbital relays and Delay-Tolerant Networking (DTN) buffering for rovers exploring dark craters.
  • Landing Safety: We looked at terrain flatness alongside proximity to Permanently Shadowed Regions (PSRs) so astronauts can land safely while staying close to water-ice deposits.

Tools, Languages & Software Used We built the platform using Python for the backend orbital math, horizon ray-casting, and data processing, paired with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript for the interactive front-end dashboard. Our data pipeline pulls directly from NASA's Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) Digital Elevation Models and NASA JPL Horizons ephemeris datasets.

Benefits, Creativity & Intended Impact What makes our project creative is how it translates heavy aerospace physics into a clean, visual decision-making dashboard that anyone can understand. Instead of digging through rows of raw coordinates, mission planners and engineers get instant answers on power budgets and communication windows. At the same time, it serves as an accessible educational tool that lets students and space fans explore the exact environmental hurdles astronauts will face when humanity returns to the Moon.
